AMBROSIO: AMERICA'S $40 TRILLION NATIONAL DEBT IS AN EXISTENTIAL THREAT AND A MAJOR DRIVER OF OUR AFFORDABILITY CRISIS

National debt has nearly quadrupled and annual interest costs have surged to $1.36 trillion during Paul Tonko's tenure in Congress

Albany, NY — [NAME], Republican candidate for Congress in New York's 20th Congressional District, is calling for urgent congressional action to confront America's exploding national debt, which he describes as the greatest long-term existential threat to the nation's economic security and a major underlying driver of the affordability crisis facing American families.

When Congressman Paul Tonko entered Congress in January 2009, the national debt stood at approximately $10 trillion. Today, it exceeds $40 trillion. Annual federal interest costs have climbed from roughly $300 billion at the beginning of his congressional tenure to approximately $1.36 trillion in fiscal year 2026.

"We have a $40 trillion national debt, and Washington is spending more than $1.3 trillion annually just on interest costs. That is an extraordinary financial burden on the American people," said [NAME]. "In my view, this is the greatest existential threat to our nation's economic future and one of the largest underlying drivers of the affordability crisis. Yet the people in Congress responsible for managing our nation's finances continue to avoid having a serious conversation about it. Paul continues to advocate for more taxes, spending, programs, subsidies, and regulations, the very policies that got us into this mess. Big government politicians like Paul Tonko are driving our economy off a cliff."

[NAME] argues that decades of deficit spending, borrowing, and fiscal mismanagement have contributed to inflationary pressures, higher interest rates, and rising costs for American households and businesses.

He also criticized Congressman Tonko's policy priorities, pointing to his public calls to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), his support for [NAME] New Deal policies, and his advocacy for expanded federal spending programs, all while our debt explodes.

"Paul Tonko has no shortage of things to talk about. He talks about abolishing ICE, [NAME] New Deals, and expanding government programs. But where is the serious discussion about the $40 trillion debt that threatens our economic future?" [NAME] asked. "How do those priorities address the enormous financial burden we are placing on American families and future generations?"

[NAME] believes the growing cost of federal debt deserves far greater attention from Congress.

"Think about this: when Paul Tonko first went to Washington, our national debt was approximately $10 trillion. Now it is over $40 trillion. We are spending more than four times as much annually on interest costs as we were around the beginning of his tenure. And what do the taxpayers of Upstate New York have to show for this staggering accumulation of debt?"

The consequences of excessive federal borrowing extend well beyond Washington. Sustained deficits can put upward pressure on interest rates, increase financing costs for homes and businesses, and crowd out private investment. Growing debt-service obligations also consume federal resources that could otherwise support national priorities or reduce future borrowing.

[NAME] is calling for reduced federal spending, regulatory reform, policies that encourage private-sector economic growth, and a credible long-term plan to stabilize the national debt.

"Every dollar Washington borrows must eventually be paid back with interest. Every dollar spent servicing debt is a dollar that is not in the pockets of the people in the 20th District," [NAME] said. "This is not sustainable, and pretending otherwise is reckless and irresponsible."

[NAME] concluded:

"The national debt is not an abstract accounting problem. It is a threat to our prosperity, our national security, and our children's future. Congress needs to stop treating this crisis as somebody else's responsibility. We need leaders who are willing to confront the problem, explain the consequences, and put forward serious solutions. The people of Upstate New York deserve nothing less. I pledge that I will address the out of control spending and debt on day one of my tenure."

💬 The Truth About the “Democrat CR”

The Democrats’ six-week “Continuing Resolution” added $10 billion in new short-term spending, plus a permanent $350 billion expansion of the Affordable Care Act.

But here’s the truth:

✅ Only about $1.5–2 billion covers truly immediate needs that keep key programs from lapsing.

❌ The rest is made up of political add-ons, one-time earmarks, or long-term policy changes that don’t belong in a six-week stopgap bill.

⚖️ Where the Money Goes

🔴 Immediate Needs — ~$1.5–2 Billion (Real, Short-Term Necessities)

These items keep vital services running temporarily until the full budget passes:

🍼 WIC Nutrition Program — ~$1.0B
Keeps benefits flowing to mothers and infants. Without it, some state WIC offices could run short by mid-October and cut off new participants.

🏥 Health & Telehealth Program Extensions — ~$0.3–0.5B
Renews funding for rural hospitals, community health centers, and telehealth waivers through Oct. 31. Without this, some programs would lose legal authority.

🎖️ Veterans Housing & Homelessness Programs — ~$0.2–0.3B
Extends VA housing assistance, suicide prevention programs, and HUD veteran housing grants for one month. Prevents temporary service gaps.

➡️ Total: ~$1.5–2 billion (short-term, legitimate needs)

🟩 Can Wait / Add-Ons — ~$8 Billion (Not Urgent)

These items aren’t emergencies — they’re discretionary or political priorities that can wait until the full appropriations process:

🏛️ Corporation for Public Broadcasting — $491 million
Advance payment to PBS/NPR that’s not due until later in FY2026.

🧾 New Inspector General at OMB — $20 million
Creates a new oversight office; useful, but not time-sensitive.

🛡️ Member Security Projects — $156 million
Adds new residential and office security systems for members of Congress; not a program continuation, just an upgrade.

⚖️ Judiciary & Facility Security — $52 million
Funds courthouse security improvements; can safely wait for the full-year budget.

⚙️ Defense & Agency Adjustments — few hundred million combined
Routine technical adjustments for the Navy, NNSA, SBA, and Treasury; both parties already agree on these, no urgency.

➡️ Total: ~$8 billion (short-term extras, not emergencies)

🟦 Permanent Policy Change — $350 Billion Over 10 Years

💊 ACA Subsidy Expansion (Permanent)

Makes the temporary COVID-era ACA premium subsidies permanent — a $350 billion, 10-year cost per the Congressional Budget Office.

That’s long-term mandatory spending being hidden inside a short-term CR.

It doesn’t fix the system — it locks in higher subsidies for insurers while costs keep rising for families.
